lines.trans: Aha! Behold this quiet historic wall—we must be right behind the clock square!
Good morning again, boss! Did you forget your wallet, or did you miss me?
Salma?! Why are you standing inside a window behind the municipal clock tower?!
Because three left turns make a circle, Rami, and this is our own kitchen window!
She is right—I am making the afternoon cinnamon rolls for Jasmine Courtyard.
So the famous two-minute shortcut brings us straight back to our own starting gate.
This is impossible! We turned north, then west, then...
And then south, right back to Jasmine Street! Give the brass compass back to Tariq.
Never mind, Salma—do you smell something burning behind you?
My cinnamon rolls! Excuse me, I have to run to the oven!
We are definitely not finding the next clue if we keep walking in circles.
Let us go back to the stone fountain and try looking at Card Two again.
This time, we follow the compass—and nobody mentions shortcuts!

meanings.note: The word 'أها' (aha) means 'aha'. It is a common interj in Levantine Arabic.

examples.text: أها! شوفوا هالحيط التاريخي الهادي—أكيد احنا بالزبط ورا ساحة الساعة!
examples.trans: Aha! Behold this quiet historic wall—we must be right behind the clock square!
This is أها.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb for 'to see, look, check' (بشوف / شاف).

examples.trans: Look inside the suitcase, Nour!
I will see you tomorrow at breakfast.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: حيطان.

examples.trans: We hung the mirror on the wall.
Stone walls keep the coolness in summer.

meanings.note: The word 'تاريخي' (el-taareekhi) means 'historic'. It is a common adj in Levantine Arabic.

examples.text: أها! شوفوا هالحيط التاريخي الهادي—أكيد احنا بالزبط ورا ساحة الساعة!
examples.trans: Aha! Behold this quiet historic wall—we must be right behind the clock square!
This is تاريخي.

meanings.note: Masculine هادي ('quiet') is homographic with the feminine demonstrative هادي ('this'); context and agreement distinguish them cleanly.

examples.trans: The spot above the tree is very quiet.
We prepared the quiet attic room for you.

meanings.note: The word 'احنا' (iHna) means 'we'. It is a common pron in Levantine Arabic.

examples.text: أها! شوفوا هالحيط التاريخي الهادي—أكيد احنا بالزبط ورا ساحة الساعة!
examples.trans: Aha! Behold this quiet historic wall—we must be right behind the clock square!
This is احنا.

meanings.note: Used almost universally in the Levantine adverbial phrase بالزبط (biz-zabt, 'exactly / right on').

examples.text: هاد هو اللون الأخضر اللي بدنا إياه بالزبط!
examples.trans: That is the exact shade of green we want!

examples.text: وصل السايق عالباب الساعة تنتين بالزبط.
examples.trans: The driver arrived at the gate at two o'clock sharp.

meanings.note: Spoken Jordanian form of وراء ('behind, past').

examples.trans: Look in the mirror behind the desk.
The hardware shop is past the bridge.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun. Plural: ساحات.

examples.trans: The courtyard has a big jasmine tree.
We sat drinking tea in the courtyard.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun. Plural: ساعات.

examples.trans: What time is it right now, please?
We arrived an hour ago on the dot.

meanings.note: Used in the universal morning greeting صباح الخير ('good morning'), answered with صباح النور.

examples.trans: Good morning! How did you sleep today?
The weather is very pleasant this morning.

meanings.note: Core word in صباح الخير ('good morning'), مساء الخير ('good evening'), تصبح على خير ('good night'), and rising-tone خير؟ ('is everything okay?').

examples.trans: Good morning, neighbours!

examples.text: خير إن شاء الله، شو صار؟
examples.trans: Hopefully all is well, what happened?

كمان.gloss: also; too; again (كمان مرة once more)

meanings.en: also; too; again (كمان مرة once more)
meanings.note: Everyday Levantine word for 'also, too, more' (كمان مرة 'one more time / again').

examples.text: التفكير السريع أنقذ الفطور كمان مرة!
examples.trans: Quick thinking saved breakfast once again!
And I missed you too.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun. Plural: مرات.

examples.trans: The doorbell rang twice.
I read the letter three times.

meanings.note: Placed directly before a name or title when addressing someone in Arabic (يا نور 'Nour!', يا أستاذ 'sir!') and in exclamations (يا سلام! 'wonderful!').

examples.trans: Good morning, Tariq!
Oh, how lovely the sun is after the rain!

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: مدراء.

examples.trans: She became the permanent front-desk manager at the guesthouse.
The manager welcomed the new guests.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بنسى, بينسى).

examples.trans: You forgot the notebook beside the soup bowl.
With all the rush, I completely forgot!

meanings.note: The word 'محفظة' (maHfaZtak) means 'your wallet'. It is a common noun in Levantine Arabic.

examples.text: صباح الخير كمان مرة يا مدير! نسيت محفظتك، ولا اشتقتلي؟
examples.trans: Good morning again, boss! Did you forget your wallet, or did you miss me?
This is محفظة.

meanings.note: With two pronunciations in context: walla ('or' in choice questions: عالشارع ولا عالساحة؟) and wala ('not even / nor': ولا خدش 'not a single scratch', ولا يهمك 'do not worry at all').

examples.trans: Is the window facing the street or the courtyard?
Not a single drop of water on the table!

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بشتاق, بيشتاق).

examples.trans: I missed you so much over these three years.
We missed our Friday gatherings.

meanings.note: The word 'سلمى' (سلمى) means 'سلمى'. It is a common noun in Levantine Arabic.

examples.text: سلمى؟! ليش واقفة جوا شباك ورا برج الساعة البلدي؟!
examples.trans: Salma?! Why are you standing inside a window behind the municipal clock tower?!
This is سلمى.

meanings.note: Spoken Jordanian question word for 'why?'.

examples.trans: Why did the person run off without his bag?
Why do you keep looking at the clock?

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian adjective (feminine: واقفة, plural: واقفين).

examples.trans: There is nobody standing in the courtyard.
They stood face to face under the tree.

meanings.note: Used both before a noun ('inside the bag') and standalone ('inside').

examples.trans: Look inside the suitcase, Nour!
The water is flowing inside!

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: شبابيك.

examples.trans: The window overlooks the courtyard tree.
We painted the wooden shutters in summer.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: أبراج.

examples.trans: The downtown clock tower is old.
We heard the tower bell at noon.

meanings.note: From بلد ('country, town'); prized on Jordanian market stalls for local olive oil, honey, lemons, and thyme.

examples.text: عسل بلدي من جبال عجلون ريحته بتشهي.
examples.trans: Local honey from the Ajloun hills smells delicious.
We bought yellow local lemons for tea.

meanings.note: Takes pronoun suffixes in spoken Jordanian: لأني (because I), لأنك (because you), لأنه (because he/it — also general 'because'), لأنكم (because you pl.).

examples.text: لأنه القهوة الطيبة بتخلي الناس لطاف!
examples.trans: Because good coffee makes people pleasant!
Thank you because you kept the bag safe.

meanings.note: The word 'تلات' (tlaat) means 'three'. It is a common noun in Levantine Arabic.

examples.text: اطنعشر دقة! أكيد هادا برج الساعة البلدي القديم تلات بلوكات لفوق!
examples.trans: Twelve chimes! That has to be the old municipal clock tower three blocks up!
This is تلات.

meanings.note: Versatile Jordanian noun meaning a wrapped parcel (اللفة البيضا), a pastry roll (لفة قرفة, also pl. لفائف), a street/stair turn (عاللفة), or a wrench turn (لفة، لفتين).

examples.text: أكلت لفة قرفة سخنة مع الشاي.
examples.trans: I ate a warm cinnamon roll with tea.
Watch the tight turn on the stairs.

meanings.note: The word 'يسار' (yasaar) means 'left'. It is a common noun in Levantine Arabic.

examples.text: يسار بعد قواوير الورد، ويسار كمان مرة بعد السور الأخضر—لوين رايحين؟!
examples.trans: Left past the flower pots, left again past the green fence—where are we going?!
This is يسار.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بعمل, بيعمل).

examples.text: اليوم رح نعمل بيض عالطريقة الفرنسية!
examples.trans: Today we will make French-style eggs!
What do we do now with the rain coming down?

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun. Plural: دوائر.

examples.trans: A paper arrived from the property department.
The department office is downtown.

meanings.note: The word 'رامي' (رامي) means 'رامي'. It is a common noun in Levantine Arabic.

examples.text: سؤال حلو، لأنه رامي بيمشي كأنه عم يلحق باص رايح!
examples.trans: Good question, because Rami walks like he is chasing a departing bus!
This is رامي.

meanings.note: The word 'هادا' (haada) means 'this'. It is a common pron in Levantine Arabic.

examples.text: بسيطة! هادا نافورة الحجر المنحوتة الصغيرة بآخر الشارع تبعنا!
examples.trans: Easy! That is the little carved stone fountain at the end of our block!
This is هادا.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: مطابخ.

examples.trans: The smell of bread is coming from the kitchen.
The guesthouse kitchen is spacious and clean.

meanings.note: Everyday preposition 'with'; takes pronoun suffixes to express 'have on one's person' (معي 'I have with me', معك حق 'you are right').

examples.trans: You are right, Nour!
Goodbye! (lit. go with safety)

meanings.note: Used in معك حق ('you are right / you have a point').

examples.trans: You are right, the weather is cold today.
Everyone has a right to rest.

meanings.note: Levantine progressive marker placed before a present-tense verb to show action happening right now.

examples.trans: The water is flowing inside the pipe right now!

examples.text: كنت عم بدور على دفتري هلا.
examples.trans: I was just looking for my notebook.

meanings.note: The word 'لفافة' (lafaa'ef) means 'rolls'. It is a common noun in Levantine Arabic.

examples.text: معها حق—أنا عم أعمل لفائف القرفة لفترة بعد الظهر لـ بيت الياسمين.
examples.trans: She is right—I am making the afternoon cinnamon rolls for Jasmine Courtyard.
This is لفافة.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun.

examples.trans: The warm scent of cinnamon filled the kitchen.
We ate a cinnamon roll with tea.

meanings.note: With demonstrative هـ + الـ, هالفترة means 'during this period / right now'.

examples.trans: I'm very busy these days.
A hard period passed over us.

meanings.note: Means 'after' (بعد المطر) and with a future span 'in' (بعد أربعين دقيقة 'in forty minutes').

examples.trans: He arrives in forty minutes.
How lovely the sun is after the rain!

meanings.note: Pronounced duhur in everyday Jordanian: الظهر means 'at noon / midday'.

examples.trans: He will arrive Friday at noon.
The sun is high at midday.

meanings.note: The word 'لـ' (لـ) means 'لـ'. It is a common noun in Levantine Arabic.

examples.text: معها حق—أنا عم أعمل لفائف القرفة لفترة بعد الظهر لـ بيت الياسمين.
examples.trans: She is right—I am making the afternoon cinnamon rolls for Jasmine Courtyard.
This is لـ.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: بيوت.

examples.trans: The old house has a lovely courtyard.
The neighbourhood houses are built of stone.

meanings.note: The word 'الياسمين' (الياسمين) means 'الياسمين'. It is a common noun in Levantine Arabic.

examples.text: شو هالصباح الحلو يوم السبت لمشية كنز بشارع شارع الياسمين!
examples.trans: What a glorious Saturday morning for a treasure walk down Jasmine Street!
This is الياسمين.

meanings.note: Used constantly in the polite phrase عن إذنك ('excuse me / with your permission').

examples.trans: Excuse me, may I pass?
He asked permission before heading out.

meanings.note: The word 'اختصار' (ikhtiSaar) means 'shortcut'. It is a common noun in Levantine Arabic.

examples.text: تلات بلوكات لفوق بالشارع الرئيسي؟ حكي فاضي، أنا بعرف اختصار بدقيقتين!
examples.trans: Three blocks up the main street? Nonsense, I know a two-minute shortcut!
This is اختصار.

meanings.note: البنت المشهورة describes Layan's high-profile popularity across school.

examples.trans: Layan is well-known across the whole school.
This is a famous restaurant in Amman.

meanings.note: Spoken Jordanian possessive word ('belonging to'); agrees in gender: تبع (m.), تبعت (f.), تبعون (pl.).

examples.text: اليوم آخر يوم بأسبوع التجربة تبعك.
examples.trans: Today is the last day of your trial week.
My brother's piano teacher!

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun. Plural: دقايق.

examples.trans: I will be back in ten minutes on the dot.
Wait one minute, please.

رجع.gloss: to return; come back; start again

meanings.en: to return; come back; start again
meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (برجع, بيرجع).

examples.trans: Can you run there and come back in ten minutes?
Did the pipe start dripping again?

meanings.note: Classic Levantine word (from Turkish doğru) meaning 'straight ahead' in directions.

examples.trans: Turn left and walk straight to the bridge.
Walk straight to the end of the street.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun. Plural: بوابات.

examples.trans: The courtyard gate is open for guests.
The taxi stopped outside the gate.

meanings.note: Invariant spoken Jordanian relative pronoun ('who, which, that') for any gender or number.

examples.trans: That is what I want.
The inn that keeps a stranger's bag safe.

meanings.note: The word 'بدي' (badeena) means 'we started'. It is a common verb in Levantine Arabic.

examples.text: إذن الاختصار المشهور تبع الدقيقتين رجعنا دغري لبوابتنا اللي بدينا منها.
examples.trans: So the famous two-minute shortcut brings us straight back to our own starting gate.
This is بدي.

meanings.note: Everyday preposition meaning 'from', 'of', or 'than' after comparatives.

examples.trans: I am Salma from the kitchen.
Breakfast is from seven-thirty to ten.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian adjective (feminine: مستحيلة, plural: —).

examples.trans: There is no way I would bother a guest with our problems!
It is impossible for us to forget this week.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بلف, بيلف).

examples.text: لفي شمال برا البوابة وامشي دغري.
examples.trans: Turn left outside the gate and walk straight.
Turn left at the stair landing.

meanings.note: In everyday Jordanian directions, شمال (shmaal) means 'left' (contrast شَمال shamaal 'north').

examples.trans: Turn left at the street corner.
The key is on the shelf to your left.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian word for 'then, next, afterwards' (وبعدين 'and then').

examples.trans: Lift the handle first, and then push.
Have some tea and then we will talk.

meanings.note: The word 'غرب' (lal-gharb) means 'to west'. It is a common noun in Levantine Arabic.

examples.text: هادا مستحيل! لفينا للشمال، بعدين للغرب، بعدين...
examples.trans: This is impossible! We turned north, then west, then...
This is غرب.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun.

examples.trans: The guests arrived from the south in the morning.
The weather is warm in the south today.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: شوارع.

examples.trans: Our guesthouse is on a quiet street in central Amman.
There are old stone streets in the quarter.

meanings.note: The word 'بوصلة' (bowSlet) means 'compass'. It is a common noun in Levantine Arabic.

examples.text: خلينا نفحص بوصلة النحاس بالأول: الشرق بروح دغري باتجاه مخبز الزاوية.
examples.trans: Let us check the brass compass first: east runs straight toward the corner bakery.
This is بوصلة.

meanings.note: In Jordanian Arabic, نحاس covers both yellow brass and red copper, often placed directly after a noun (مفاتيح نحاس brass keys).

examples.trans: We polished the brass keys in the morning.
The brass pot is old and engraved.

meanings.note: The word 'طارق' (طارق) means 'طارق'. It is a common noun in Levantine Arabic.

examples.text: أنا ساكن بشارع شارع الياسمين من عشرين سنة يا طارق، والزقاق بيغلب البوصلة!
examples.trans: I have lived on Jasmine Street for twenty years, Tariq, and alleys beat compasses!
This is طارق.

meanings.note: Negates nouns, adjectives, participles, and pronouns in spoken Jordanian (مش شنتتي 'not my bag', مش ملاقي 'cannot find').

examples.trans: This is not my suitcase!
Not bad for a second day at work!

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian adjective (feminine: مهمة, plural: مهمين).

examples.text: يوم الجمعة يوم مهم كتير إلي.
examples.trans: Friday is a very important day for me.
I have an important note at the bottom of the page.

meanings.note: The word 'سلمى—شامة' (سلمى—شامة) means 'سلمى—شامة'. It is a common noun in Levantine Arabic.

examples.text: مش مهم يا سلمى—شامة ريحة إشي عم ينحرق وراكي؟
examples.trans: Never mind, Salma—do you smell something burning behind you?
This is سلمى—شامة.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun. Plural: روايح.

examples.trans: The aroma of coffee in the morning is wonderful!
The scent of cinnamon reaches the second floor.

meanings.note: The typical Jordanian form of شي: في إشي؟ 'is something wrong?', ولا إشي 'nothing at all'.

examples.text: في إشي بدك إياه من السوق؟
examples.trans: Is there anything you want from the market?
Nothing happened at all, relax.

meanings.note: The word 'انحرق' (yinHareq) means 'it burns'. It is a common verb in Levantine Arabic.

examples.text: مش مهم يا سلمى—شامة ريحة إشي عم ينحرق وراكي؟
examples.trans: Never mind, Salma—do you smell something burning behind you?
This is انحرق.

meanings.note: Means 'about' (عن الزبدة), 'off / away from' (عن جبيني), and appears in عن جد ('really!') and عن إذنك ('excuse me').

examples.trans: I will carry the suitcase up for you.
I heard your voices about the butter!

meanings.note: Invariant modal word followed by a subjunctive verb (without ب-) to express 'must / have to / need to'.

examples.trans: Tell me everything I need to know.
Everything has to be just right!

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun.

examples.trans: She came running back across the overpass in ten minutes.
Running in the morning energises the body.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: أفران.

examples.text: لفائف القرفة طلعت من الفرن هلا.
examples.trans: The cinnamon rolls just came out of the oven.
The bakery down the street bakes in the morning.

meanings.note: Means 'certainly, definitely' or 'must be' (إنتي أكيد نور 'you must be Nour').

examples.trans: Hello! You must be Nour.

examples.text: أكيد صاحبه رح يدور عليه قريبا.
examples.trans: Surely its owner will look for it soon.

meanings.note: Invariant spoken Levantine future marker placed before a subjunctive verb (without ب-).

examples.text: ضيفة غرفة أربعة رح تقعد كل الأسبوع.
examples.trans: Room four's guest will stay all week.

examples.text: تاني يوم ما رح يكون ممل!
examples.trans: The second day is not going to be boring!

meanings.note: The word 'لاقى' (nlaaqeeh) means 'we find it'. It is a common verb in Levantine Arabic.

examples.text: هلق شوفوا منيح عالكرت الأول عشان نشوف شو الرمز اللي لازم نلاقيه.
examples.trans: Now look closely at Card One to see what symbol we need to find.
This is لاقى.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: أدلة.

examples.trans: I bought the Amman travel guide.
The guesthouse is listed in the annual guide.

meanings.note: Active participle of إجا ('to come'): means 'on the way / arriving' (جايين 'they are coming') and after a time noun 'next' (الأسبوع الجاي 'next week').

examples.trans: The guests are coming down the stairs now.
We will see you next week!

meanings.note: Everyday conditional word 'if' for real possibilities.

examples.text: رني الجرس إذا احتجتي أي شي.
examples.trans: Ring the bell if you need anything.

examples.text: إذا فتحنا الساحة الصبح، الجيران بيفرحوا.
examples.trans: If we open the courtyard in the morning, the neighbours will be delighted.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بضل, بيضل).

examples.trans: Family is what remains.
My teacup stayed intact inside the suitcase!

meanings.note: Common defective verb for walking on foot or things running smoothly.

examples.text: ممنوع تمشي عكاحلك لحد بكرا الصبح.
examples.trans: You mustn't walk on your ankle until tomorrow morning.

examples.text: مشينا عالهدا بالساحة بعد ما وقفت المطر.
examples.trans: We walked gently across the courtyard after the rain stopped.

meanings.note: Imperative forms with object pronouns give خليكم بحالكم ('stay in your own business') and خلوني بحالي ('leave me in mine').

examples.trans: Let me speak for a bit.
Stay calm, Mariam.

meanings.note: The word 'نافورة' (nafooret) means 'fountain'. It is a common noun in Levantine Arabic.

examples.text: بسيطة! هادا نافورة الحجر المنحوتة الصغيرة بآخر الشارع تبعنا!
examples.trans: Easy! That is the little carved stone fountain at the end of our block!
This is نافورة.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: حجار.

examples.trans: Old stone holds warmth.
She stepped onto the stone step outside.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بحاول, بيحاول).

examples.trans: I tried to smile as hard as I could!
We tried to find a quick solution.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: كروت.

examples.text: بعتتله كرت بريد قصير الأسبوع الماضي.
examples.trans: I sent him a short postcard last week.
I recognised his neat handwriting on the card right away.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian adjective (feminine: تانية, plural: تانيين).

examples.trans: Room four is on the second floor.
There is a second sheet behind the letter.

meanings.note: The word 'اتبع' (itba3oo) means 'follow'. It is a common verb in Levantine Arabic.

examples.text: خليني أقرأ الكرت التاني: اتبعوا الورقة لحد ما اطنعشر دقة ترمي خيال مستقيم.
examples.trans: Let me read Card Two: Follow the leaf until twelve chimes cast a straight shadow.
This is اتبع.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بجيب, بيجيب).

examples.text: رح أجيب شراشف نظيفة من الخزانة.
examples.trans: I will bring clean sheets from the closet.

examples.text: أي علبة زبدة جبتي يا نور؟
examples.trans: Which tub of butter did you bring, Nour?

meanings.note: Used in جاب سيرة ('to bring up / mention a topic').

examples.text: لا حدا يجيب سيرة الشغل عالعشا!
examples.trans: Nobody bring up work at dinner!
Everyone speaks kindly of you.

إلى.gloss: to; until (إلى اللقاء see you soon)

meanings.en: to; until (إلى اللقاء see you soon)
meanings.note: Appears in everyday speech inside warm set phrases such as إلى اللقاء! ('until we meet again!').

examples.trans: See you soon, sir!
Goodbye and until next time.

meanings.note: The word 'اللقاء' (اللقاء) means 'اللقاء'. It is a common noun in Levantine Arabic.

examples.trans: Goodbye!
This is اللقاء.
